extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of medieval Italian political history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting normative lessons and institutional standards from a historical narrative of 14th-century Siena — how magistracies, factional law, procedures, and use of force affected stability and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional procedure for official communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Official acts (e.g., opening and reading letters) must follow the constitutionally required procedure — 'without calling in the college of the twelve, as, according to the constitution, they ought to have done, opened and read it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recounts that opening a false letter without summoning the college provoked nobles, led to the hanging of the messenger, mass disturbances, and further politicized conflict; procedural violations provoked escalation and loss of legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on noble authority and avoidance of arbitrariness
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities must avoid arbitrary exercise of office by nobles whose birth and wealth give them excessive influence — 'The noblemen proceeded in their offices too arbitrarily; the splendor of their birth and riches ... acquired them too much credit ... and ... they must needs govern all things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When nobles used their prestige to seize public arms or dominate offices (sometimes to 'satisfy their own ambition'), popular resentment and civil strife followed. Offices should be exercised for 'the honour and utility of the state' rather than private aggrandizement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for regular legal process and formality of trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishments, imprisonments, and confiscations should occur under regular process of law and formal trials — the critic: many actions were done 'without any regular process of law or formality of trial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative links absence of due process to mass punishments, imprisonments, beheadings, and long-term injustice; lack of legal formality undermined legitimacy and produced persistent unrest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not legalize factional divisions (avoid institutionalizing factions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation and magistracies should not be expressly built on factional distributions or permanent partisan distinctions — 'by creating magistrates expressly and avowedly by distributions of factions ... they made their discords immortal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making factional divisions part of the constitution (naming 'people of the greater number', 'middle number', etc., and allocating offices by faction) preserved and perpetuated divisions across generations, producing continuing violence and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of executive power to prevent tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid concentrating sovereignty and executive authority in a single assembly or person; moving to one-assembly rule invites domination and rivalry — 'of what avail are treaties ... when the government remains in one assembly?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The history argues that concentrating government in one assembly (or conversely, improper separation) enables rival families to vie for supremacy and ultimately destroys the commonwealth; institutional balance is required to prevent domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to statutory limits on criminal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials exercising criminal authority must observe statutory limits and procedures; discretionary, extra-statutory criminal power is dangerous — the text notes an Executor given 'great authority in criminal matters, even to proceed discretionally, and without observing the orders of the statutes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting wide discretionary criminal powers led to corruption, summary executions, and breakdown of justice; unlawful discretion undermined rule of law and failed to secure public order in the long term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on foreign arms to settle domestic conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic factions should not secure their position primarily through foreign military intervention or foreign-backed commanders (e.g., seeking the emperor's or pope's armed support).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account shows reliance on imperial or foreign troops (Malatesta, imperial forces) produced massacres, plunder, and loss of autonomous control; foreign intervention resolved immediate contests but deepened domestic treachery and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden eligibility for magistracies to prevent oligarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Confining selection of magistrates to a narrow set (e.g., 'choice of magistrates was confined to fifty persons only') establishes an oligarchy that damages the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When offices become restricted to a small elite, political exclusion breeds factional rivalry, revolt, and ultimately weakening or destruction of the state; inclusiveness in selection reduces oligarchic capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid political rewards for betrayal; maintain legitimacy of appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not consolidate power by rewarding individuals or families for treachery with privileges or elevated civic status (e.g., giving castles and making them 'popular citizens' as recompense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recounts the Salimbeni being rewarded with castles and popular status for their role — such patronage undermines legitimacy of institutions and deepens factional resentment that fuels future conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper division between civil and criminal jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve clear boundaries between civil and criminal authority (the narrative notes officials with 'full authority ... and a discretionary power in all criminal cases, but not in civil').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blurring civil and criminal roles or granting extraordinary criminal jurisdiction to officials meant for civil administration led to abuses, arbitrary punishments, and erosion of legitimate governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and restraint in popular assemblies to prevent shortsighted choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Unstructured popular assemblies and ephemeral mass passions ('scrambling for loaves and fishes') lead to shortsighted, self-interested decisions harmful to the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Scrambling for loaves and fishes, in an assembly of people ... will for ever have the same effects' — the crowd's inconstancy makes them susceptible to demagogy and immediate gain, so institutional checks and durable frameworks are necessary to temper popular impulses.
